title: حِكَايَةُ قَمَرِ الزَّمَانِ
source: William Hay Macnaghten, ed., The Alif Laila, or Book of the Thousand Nights and One Night, vol. 2, Calcutta 1839 (“Calcutta II”), printed pp. 28–31 (Night 234, continuing nights-233), transcribed from the scan (archive.org aliflailaorbook02unkngoog) by the editors' own transcription. The edition prints the prose essentially unpointed: ALL VOCALIZATION (tashkīl) IS EDITORIAL — ours, not the edition's — and the alphabet button strips it back to the bare rasm as Macnaghten prints it, except where a clear misprint has been corrected (each is noted). Romanization is simplified IJMES. Spelling, including the edition’s Middle Arabic forms, is preserved; clear misprints are corrected in the text, and the note on each gives the print’s reading. Obscure or doubtful forms are kept as printed, vocalized by evident sense and flagged in the notes. Read-aloud audio is a Modern Standard Arabic reading of this vocalised text, synthesized by machine, with word-by-word timing generated the same way.
about: Night 234 continues the tale of Qamar al-Zamān. Bahrām the Magian ships al-Asʿad off locked in a chest; al-Amjad, watching the sea, has the ship searched in vain, and at home finds two lines of verse on a wall that make him weep for his brother. A storm drives the ship off course to a city on the shore ruled by Queen Marjāna. Bahrām passes al-Asʿad off as his last mamlūk; the queen, moved by his tears and by the verses he writes for her, takes him from Bahrām by force and orders the Magian to sail from her land that very night. She feasts al-Asʿad in her castle above the sea, and morning overtakes Shahrazād. As with every printed edition of the Nights, this one belongs to the late Egyptian recension (ZER) — an eighteenth-century expansion padded out to a literal 1001 nights; no printed edition is a medieval text, and Macnaghten regularised the language here and there, so some Middle Arabic texture is a nineteenth-century retrofit.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا كَانَتِ اللَّيْلَةُ الرَّابِعَةُ وَالثَّلٰثُونَ بَعْدَ الْمِائَتَيْنِ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā kānati al-laylatu al-rābiʿatu wa-al-thalāthūna baʿda al-miʾatayni
sentences.l: And when it was the night, the fourth and the thirty after the two-hundred,
sentences.i: And when it was the two hundred and thirty-fourth night,
sentences.n: The night's opening formula: the unit, al-rābiʿatu, comes first and is joined to the tens by wa-, all nominative in agreement with al-laylatu. thalāthūn is printed without its middle alif, with the dagger alif already set; the ئ of المائتين is printed.

sentences.t: قَالَتْ بَلَغَنِي أَيُّهَا الْمَلِكُ السَّعِيدُ أَنَّ بَهْرَامَ الْمَجُوسِيَّ لَمَّا جَهَّزَ مَرْكَبًا لِلسَّفَرِ أَخَذَ الْأَسْعَدَ وَحَطَّهُ فِي صُنْدُوقٍ وَقَفَلَهُ عَلَيْهِ وَنَقَلَهُ إِلَى الْمَرْكَبِ
sentences.tr: qālat balaghanī ayyuhā al-maliku al-saʿīdu anna Bahrāma al-Majūsiyya lammā jahhaza markaban li-al-safari akhadha al-Asʿada wa-ḥaṭṭahu fī ṣundūqin wa-qafalahu ʿalayhi wa-naqalahu ilā al-markabi
sentences.l: She-said: It-has-reached-me, O fortunate king, that Bahrām the-Magian, when he-fitted-out a-ship for-the-journey, took al-Asʿad and-put-him in a-chest and-locked-it upon-him and-carried-it to the-ship.
sentences.i: She said: It has reached me, O fortunate king, that when Bahrām the Magian had fitted out a ship for the voyage, he took al-Asʿad, put him in a chest, locked it on him and carried it on board.
sentences.n: jahhaza, Form II, 'to equip, fit out'; its shadda is printed, as is the shadda of حطّه. li-al-safari, 'for the journey': li- of purpose. ḥaṭṭa, 'to put, set down', is the everyday verb of the Nights where Classical prose says waḍaʿa. qafalahu ʿalayhi, 'he locked it upon him': the suffix of qafala is the chest, and ʿalā marks the one shut inside it. The fatḥa on الاسعدَ is printed, marking it as the object of akhadha. Bahrām is a diptote, the noun of anna, so -a without tanwīn.

sentences.t: وَكَانَ فِي تِلْكَ السَّاعَةِ الَّتِي حَوَّلَ فِيهَا بَهْرَامُ الصُّنْدُوقَ الَّذِي فِيهِ الْأَسْعَدُ كَانَ الْأَمْجَدُ بِالْقَضَاءِ وَالْقَدَرِ وَاقِفًا يَتَفَرَّجُ عَلَى الْبَحْرِ
sentences.tr: wa-kāna fī tilka al-sāʿati allatī ḥawwala fīhā Bahrāmu al-ṣundūqa alladhī fīhi al-Asʿadu kāna al-Amjadu bi-al-qaḍāʾi wa-al-qadari wāqifan yatafarraju ʿalā al-baḥri
sentences.l: And-it-was, in that the-hour in-which moved Bahrām the-chest which in-it (was) al-Asʿad, was al-Amjad, by-the-decree and-the-destiny, standing looking-out over the-sea.
sentences.i: Now it so happened that at the very hour when Bahrām was moving the chest with al-Asʿad in it, al-Amjad, as fate and destiny would have it, was standing gazing out over the sea.
sentences.n: The sentence opens with wa-kāna, 'and it was (that)', and then, after the long time clause, starts again with a second kāna that carries the real subject, al-Amjad: a loose, spoken build, kept as it is. ḥawwala, Form II, 'to move, shift'; its shadda is printed, as is that of يتفرّج. bi-al-qaḍāʾi wa-al-qadari, 'by the decree and the destiny': bi- of cause, 'as God had decreed'; the hamza of القضاء is printed. tafarraja ʿalā, 'to look on at, take in the sight of': ʿalā marks what is looked at.

sentences.t: فَنَظَرَ الْأَمْجَدُ إِلَى الْحَوَائِجِ وَهُمْ يَنْقُلُونَهَا إِلَي الْمَرْكَبِ فَخَفَقَ فُؤَادُهُ
sentences.tr: fa-naẓara al-Amjadu ilā al-ḥawāʾiji wa-hum yanqulūnahā ilā al-markabi fa-khafaqa fuʾāduhu
sentences.l: And-looked al-Amjad at the-goods, and-they (were) carrying-them to the-ship, and-throbbed his-heart.
sentences.i: Al-Amjad saw the baggage being carried on board, and his heart fluttered.
sentences.n: ḥawāʾij, plural of ḥāja, 'needs', here 'things, gear, baggage', a common sense in the Nights; the ئ is printed. wa-hum yanqulūnahā, 'while they were carrying them': a circumstantial clause, its 'they' the porters, never named. إلي is printed with a dotted ي; kept as set. The ؤ of فؤاده is printed.

sentences.t: وَأَمَرَ غِلْمَانَهُ أَنْ يُقَدِّمُوا لَهُ مَرْكُوبَهُ
sentences.tr: wa-amara ghilmānahu an yuqaddimū lahu markūbahu
sentences.l: And-he-ordered his-pages that they-bring-forward for-him his-mount.
sentences.i: He ordered his pages to bring him his horse.
sentences.n: amara with an, 'to order (someone) to'. qaddama, Form II, 'to bring forward, set before'; its shadda is printed. li- marks the one it is brought for. markūb, 'what is ridden', a mount.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ رَكِبَ فِي جُمْلَةٍ مِنْ جَمَاعَتِهِ وَتَوَجَّهَ إِلَى الْبَحْرِ وَوَقَفَ عَلَى مَرْكَبِ الْمَجُوسِيِّ
sentences.tr: thumma rakiba fī jumlatin min jamāʿatihi wa-tawajjaha ilā al-baḥri wa-waqafa ʿalā markabi al-Majūsiyyi
sentences.l: Then he-rode in a-body of his-company, and-headed to the-sea, and-stood at (the) ship (of) the-Magian.
sentences.i: Then he rode out with a body of his men, made for the shore and halted beside the Magian's ship.
sentences.n: fī jumlatin min, 'in a number of': fī marks those he rides among. waqafa ʿalā, 'to stand over, stop at'. The shadda of توجّه is printed.

sentences.t: وَأَمَرَ مَنْ مَعَهُ أَنْ يَنْزِلُوا الْمَرْكَبَ وَيُفَتِّشُوهَا فَنَزَلَتِ الرِّجَالُ وَفَتَّشُوا الْمَرْكَبَ جَمِيعَهَا فَلَمْ يَجِدُوا فِيهَا شَيْأً
sentences.tr: wa-amara man maʿahu an yanzilū al-markaba wa-yufattishūhā fa-nazalati al-rijālu wa-fattashū al-markaba jamīʿahā fa-lam yajidū fīhā shayʾan
sentences.l: And-he-ordered whoever (was) with-him that they-go-down (into) the-ship and-search-her; and-went-down the-men and-searched the-ship, all-of-her, but-not they-found in-her a-thing.
sentences.i: He ordered those with him to go down into the ship and search her. The men went aboard and searched the whole ship, but found nothing in her.
sentences.n: markab is masculine in Classical Arabic, but here it takes feminine pronouns, يفتشوها, جميعها, فيها, as ships often do in the Nights; kept as the text has it. nazala, 'to go down', takes the ship as a direct object, 'go down into, board'. fa-nazalati al-rijālu: a feminine verb before a broken plural of persons, which the grammar allows. The shaddas of يفتّشوها and فتّشوا are printed. شيأ is the edition's spelling of shayʾan, with the hamza printed.

sentences.t: فَطَلَعُوا وَأَعْلَمُوا الْأَمْجَدَ بِذٰلِكَ فَرَكِبَ وَوَلَّى طَالِبًا بَيْتَهُ
sentences.tr: fa-ṭalaʿū wa-aʿlamū al-Amjada bi-dhālika fa-rakiba wa-wallā ṭāliban baytahu
sentences.l: And-they-came-up and-informed al-Amjad of-that; and-he-mounted and-turned-away seeking his-house.
sentences.i: They came back up and told al-Amjad so, and he mounted and turned away, making for home.
sentences.n: ṭalaʿa, 'to come up', the opposite of nazala above: up out of the ship. aʿlama bi-, 'to inform of': bi- marks what is made known. wallā, 'to turn away, depart'; its shadda is printed. ṭāliban baytahu, 'seeking his house', an accusative of state. dhālika takes a dagger alif.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا وَصَلَ إِلَى مَنْزِلِهِ وَدَخَلَ الْقَصْرَ انْقَبَضَ خَاطِرُهُ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā waṣala ilā manzilihi wa-dakhala al-qaṣra inqabaḍa khāṭiruhu
sentences.l: And-when he-arrived at his-dwelling and-entered the-palace, was-contracted his-mind.
sentences.i: When he reached his dwelling and entered the palace, a heaviness came over his spirits.
sentences.n: The print has القبض خاطرة, misprints for انقبض خاطره, corrected here: ل set for ن in the verb, and ة for the pronoun suffix ه in the noun. inqabaḍa khāṭiruhu, 'his mind was oppressed', Form VII of qabaḍa, 'to grip', is the stock phrase for a sinking heart. khāṭir, 'mind, thoughts, spirits'.

sentences.t: فَنَظَرَ بِعَيْنِهِ فِى الدَّارِ فَرَأَى سَطْرَيْنِ مَكْتُوبَيْنِ عَلَى حَائِطٍ وَهُمَا هٰذَانِ الْبَيْتَانِ
sentences.tr: fa-naẓara bi-ʿaynihi fī al-dāri fa-raʾā saṭrayni maktūbayni ʿalā ḥāʾiṭin wa-humā hādhāni al-baytāni
sentences.l: And-he-looked with-his-eye in the-house, and-saw two-lines written on a-wall, and-they-two (were) these-two the-two-verses:
sentences.i: He cast his eye about the house and saw two lines written on a wall, and these were the two verses:
sentences.n: naẓara bi-ʿaynihi, 'he looked with his eye': bi- of the instrument. فى is printed with ى, and فراى with a bare alif; both kept as set. The ئ of حائط is printed. hādhāni, the dual demonstrative, takes a dagger alif; bayt is a line of verse.

sentences.t:
اَحْبَابُنَا اِنْ غِبْتُمُ عَنْ نَاظِرِيْ * فَعَنِ الْفُؤَادِ وَخَاطِرِيْ مَا غِبْتُمُ
لٰكِنَّكُمْ خَلَّفْتُمُونِي مُدْنِفًا * وَمَنَعْتُمُ جَفْنِي الرُّقَادَ وَنِمْتُمُ
sentences.tr:
aḥbābunā in ghibtumu ʿan nāẓirī * fa-ʿani al-fuʾādi wa-khāṭirī mā ghibtumu
lākinnakum khallaftumūnī mudnifan * wa-manaʿtumu jafniya al-ruqāda wa-nimtumu
sentences.l:
Our-beloved-ones, if you-are-absent from my-sight, * then-from the-heart and-my-mind not you-are-absent;
but-you left-me-behind wasting-with-sickness, * and-you-denied my-eyelid the-sleep, and-you-slept.
sentences.i:
Beloved, though you have vanished from my sight, * from my heart and my thoughts you have never gone;
yet you have left me behind, sick and wasting, * and robbed my eyelids of sleep, while you slept on.
sentences.n: The verse is pointed in the print and copied as printed. The rhyme falls on -tumu, ghibtumu / nimtumu, the final mīm given a ḍamma for the metre, as again in manaʿtumu and the first ghibtumu. The print sets a sukūn on the long ī of ناظري and خاطري. mudnif, 'wasted by long sickness', the lover's stock condition. manaʿa takes two objects, the one denied and the thing denied: jafniya, 'my eyelid', and al-ruqāda, 'sleep'.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا قَرَأَهُمَا الْأَمْجَدُ تَذَكَّرَ أَخَاهُ وَبَكَى
sentences.tr: fa-lammā qaraʾahumā al-Amjadu tadhakkara akhāhu wa-bakā
sentences.l: And-when read-them-two al-Amjad, he-remembered his-brother and-wept.
sentences.i: When al-Amjad read them, he remembered his brother and wept.
sentences.n: The print has اخاة, a misprint for اخاه, corrected here: akhāhu, 'his brother', accusative of the five nouns. The hamza of قرأهما and the shadda of تذكّر are printed.

sentences.t: هٰذَا مَاكَانَ مِنْ أَمْرِهِ
sentences.tr: hādhā mā kāna min amrihi
sentences.l: This (is) what was of his-affair.
sentences.i: So much for him.
sentences.n: The formula of transition between two threads of the tale; the print runs mā kāna together, ماكان, as it does again in the next line; kept as set.

sentences.t: وَأَمَّا مَاكَانَ مِنْ أَمْرِ بَهْرَامَ الْمَجُوسِيِّ فَإِنَّهُ نَزَلَ الْمَرْكَبَ وَصَاحَ وَزَعَقَ عَلَى الْبَحْرِيَّةِ أَنْ يُعَجِّلُوا بِحَلِّ الْقُلُوعِ
sentences.tr: wa-ammā mā kāna min amri Bahrāma al-Majūsiyyi fa-innahu nazala al-markaba wa-ṣāḥa wa-zaʿaqa ʿalā al-baḥriyyati an yuʿajjilū bi-ḥalli al-qulūʿi
sentences.l: And-as-for what was of (the) affair (of) Bahrām the-Magian, then-indeed-he went-down (into) the-ship and-shouted and-bawled at the-sailors that they-hasten with-loosing the-sails.
sentences.i: As for Bahrām the Magian, he went aboard and shouted and bawled at the crew to make haste and loose the sails.
sentences.n: Bahrāma, a diptote, takes -a for the genitive after amri. ṣāḥa wa-zaʿaqa, 'shouted and bawled', a doubling for emphasis; zaʿaqa ʿalā, 'to bawl at': ʿalā marks the one shouted at. al-baḥriyya, 'the sea-folk', the crew, a collective. ʿajjala bi-, 'to hasten with': bi- marks the thing hurried. ḥall al-qulūʿ, 'the untying of the sails', setting them loose to the wind; qulūʿ is plural of qilʿ, 'sail'. The shaddas of يعجّلوا and بحلّ are printed.

sentences.t: فَحَلُّوا الْقُلُوعَ وَسَافَرُوا وَلَمْ يَزَالُوا مُسَافِرِينَ أَيَّامًا وَلَيَالِيَ
sentences.tr: fa-ḥallū al-qulūʿa wa-sāfarū wa-lam yazālū musāfirīna ayyāman wa-layāliya
sentences.l: And-they-loosed the-sails and-set-out, and-not they-ceased travelling (for) days and-nights.
sentences.i: So they loosed the sails and set out, and they sailed on for days and nights.
sentences.n: lam yazālū with an active participle, 'they did not cease travelling', so 'they kept on'. ayyāman wa-layāliya, accusative of time; layālī is a diptote, so -iya without tanwīn. The shadda of فحلّوا is printed.

sentences.t: وَبَعْدَ كُلِّ يَوْمَيْنِ يُخْرِجُ الْأَسْعَدَ وَيُطْعِمُهُ قَلِيلًا مِنَ الزَّادِ وَيَسْقِيهِ قَلِيلًا مِنَ الْمَاءِ إِلَى أَنْ قَرُبُوا مِنْ جَبَلِ النَّارِ
sentences.tr: wa-baʿda kulli yawmayni yukhriju al-Asʿada wa-yuṭʿimuhu qalīlan mina al-zādi wa-yasqīhi qalīlan mina al-māʾi ilā an qarubū min jabali al-nāri
sentences.l: And-after every two-days he-brings-out al-Asʿad and-feeds-him a-little of the-provisions and-gives-him-to-drink a-little of the-water, until that they-drew-near to (the) Mountain (of) the-Fire.
sentences.i: Every second day Bahrām would bring al-Asʿad out and give him a little of the provisions to eat and a little water to drink, until they drew near the Mountain of Fire.
sentences.n: The subject of yukhriju is Bahrām, left unnamed. The imperfects, yukhriju, yuṭʿimuhu, yasqīhi, are habitual, 'he would bring out'. yukhriju is Form IV, 'to bring out', from the chest. ilā an, 'until', here with a perfect, qarubū, 'they drew near'; qaruba min, 'to come near to'. jabal al-nār, 'the Mountain of Fire', which they will not reach.

sentences.t: فَخَرَجَ عَلَيْهِمْ رِيحٌ وَهَاجَ بِهِمُ الْبَحْرُ فَتَاهَتِ الْمَرْكَبُ عَنِ الطَّرِيقِ وَسَلَكُوا طَرِيقًا غَيْرَ طَرِيقِهِمْ وَعَبَرُوا إِلَى بَحْرٍ غَيْرِهِ
sentences.tr: fa-kharaja ʿalayhim rīḥun wa-hāja bihimu al-baḥru fa-tāhati al-markabu ʿani al-ṭarīqi wa-salakū ṭarīqan ghayra ṭarīqihim wa-ʿabarū ilā baḥrin ghayrihi
sentences.l: And-came-out against-them a-wind, and-raged with-them the-sea, and-strayed the-ship from the-way; and-they-took a-way other-than their-way, and-crossed to a-sea other-than-it.
sentences.i: Then a wind sprang up against them and the sea rose under them, and the ship strayed from her course; they took a course other than their own and passed into another sea.
sentences.n: rīḥ, 'wind', is feminine in Classical Arabic, but here takes the masculine verb kharaja; the ship is feminine again, tāhat. kharaja ʿalā, 'to come out against': ʿalā marks those it falls upon. hāja bihim, 'raged with them': bi- marks those it carried along. tāha ʿan, 'to stray from'. baḥrin ghayrihi, 'a sea other than it', that is, another sea; ghayr agrees in case with baḥrin.

sentences.t: وَوَصَلُوا إِلَى مَدِينَةٍ مَبْنِيَّةٍ عَلَى شَاطِئِ الْبَحْرِ وَلَهَا قَلْعَةٌ بِشَبَابِيكَ تُطِلُّ عَلَى تِلْكَ الْبَحْرِ
sentences.tr: wa-waṣalū ilā madīnatin mabniyyatin ʿalā shāṭiʾi al-baḥri wa-lahā qalʿatun bi-shabābīka tuṭillu ʿalā tilka al-baḥri
sentences.l: And-they-arrived at a-city built on (the) shore (of) the-sea, and-to-it (was) a-castle with-windows overlooking that the-sea.
sentences.i: They came to a city built on the shore of the sea, with a castle whose windows looked out over that sea.
sentences.n: lahā, 'to it', li- of possession: 'it had a citadel'. bi-shabābīka, 'with windows': bi- of accompaniment, 'having windows'; shabābīk, plural of shubbāk, is a diptote, so -a without tanwīn. aṭalla ʿalā, Form IV, 'to look down upon, overlook'; the verb agrees with the citadel or with the windows, both feminine. tilka al-baḥri, 'that sea', with the feminine demonstrative before the masculine baḥr; kept as the text has it. The shaddas of مبنيّة and تطلّ and the ئ of شاطئ are printed.

sentences.t: وَالْحَاكِمَةُ عَلَى تِلْكَ الْمَدِينَةِ امْرَأَةٌ يُقَالُ لَهَا الْمَلِكَةُ مَرْجَانَةُ
sentences.tr: wa-al-ḥākimatu ʿalā tilka al-madīnati imraʾatun yuqālu lahā al-Malikatu Marjānatu
sentences.l: And-the-ruling-one over that the-city (was) a-woman, (it) is-said to-her: the-Queen Marjāna.
sentences.i: And the ruler of that city was a woman called Queen Marjāna.
sentences.n: ḥakama ʿalā, 'to rule over': ʿalā marks what is ruled. yuqālu lahā, 'it is said to her', the usual way of giving a name: 'who was called'; li- marks the one named. Marjāna, from marjān, 'coral', is a diptote, so -u without tanwīn. The hamza of امرأة is printed.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ الرَّئِيسُ لِبَهْرَامَ يَاسَيِّدِي إِنَّنَا تِهْنَا عَنِ الطَّرِيقِ وَلَابُدَّ لَنَا مِنَ الدُّخُولِ إِلَى هٰذِهِ الْمَدِينَةِ لِأَجْلِ الرَّاحَةِ وَبَعْدَ ذٰلِكَ يَفْعَلُ اللّٰهُ مَايَشَاءُ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla al-raʾīsu li-Bahrāma yā sayyidī innanā tihnā ʿani al-ṭarīqi wa-lā budda lanā mina al-dukhūli ilā hādhihi al-madīnati li-ajli al-rāḥati wa-baʿda dhālika yafʿalu allāhu mā yashāʾu
sentences.l: And-said the-captain to-Bahrām: O my-lord, indeed-we have-strayed from the-way, and-no escape for-us from the-entering into this the-city for-the-sake-of the-rest; and-after that God does what He-wills.
sentences.i: Then the captain said to Bahrām, “My lord, we have lost our way, and we cannot but put in at this city to rest; after that, God will do what He wills.”
sentences.n: The print has ابهرام, a misprint for لبهرام, corrected here: li-Bahrāma, 'to Bahrām', li- marking the one spoken to, as everywhere else with qāla. (A vocative a-Bahrāmu, 'O Bahrām', is conceivable in Classical Arabic, but it is not how this text addresses anyone, and yā sayyidī follows at once.) al-raʾīs, 'the head', is the ship's master, the captain; its ئ is printed. tihnā, 'we have strayed', from tāha, yatīhu, as in fa-tāhat al-markabu just before. lā budda li- … min, 'there is no escape for … from', so 'must'. Printed run together, ياسيدي and مايشاء, and the shadda of لابدّ is printed; kept as set. Bahrām is a diptote, so li-Bahrāma, genitive in -a.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ لَهُ بَهْرَامُ نِعْمَ مَا فَعَلْتَ وَمَا رَأَيْتَ وَالَّذِي تَرَاهُ افْعَلْهُ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla lahu Bahrāmu niʿma mā faʿalta wa-mā raʾayta wa-alladhī tarāhu ifʿalhu
sentences.l: And-said to-him Bahrām: Excellent (is) what you-did and-what you-saw; and-that-which you-see-it, do-it.
sentences.i: Bahrām said to him, “You have done well and judged well; whatever you think fit, do it.”
sentences.n: niʿma mā, 'how excellent is what …', the verb of praise niʿma with mā; Classical often writes it as one word, نعمّا. raʾā here is 'to judge, think best', as in tarāhu, 'what you see (fit)'. The hamza of رأيت is printed.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ لَهُ الرَّئِيسُ إِذَا أَرْسَلَتْ لَنَا الْمَلِكَةُ تَسْأَلُنَا مَاذَا يَكُونُ جَوَابُنَا لَهَا
sentences.tr: fa-qāla lahu al-raʾīsu idhā arsalat lanā al-malikatu tasʾalunā mādhā yakūnu jawābunā lahā
sentences.l: And-said to-him the-captain: When sends to-us the-queen asking-us, what will-be our-answer to-her?
sentences.i: “And if the queen sends to question us,” the captain asked him, “what answer shall we give her?”
sentences.n: arsala li-, 'to send to': li- marks the one sent to; tasʾalunā, 'asking us', says what the queen sends to do, with no 'to' between, as often. The hamza of تسألنا is printed.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ لَهُ بَهْرَامُ أَنَا عِنْدِي هٰذَا الْمُسْلِمُ الَّذِي مَعَنَا فَنُلْبِسُهُ لِبْسَ الْمَمَالِيكِ وَنُخْرِجُهُ مَعَنَا
sentences.tr: fa-qāla lahu Bahrāmu anā ʿindī hādhā al-muslimu alladhī maʿanā fa-nulbisuhu libsa al-mamālīki wa-nukhrijuhu maʿanā
sentences.l: And-said to-him Bahrām: I, with-me (is) this the-Muslim who (is) with-us; so-we-clothe-him (in the) clothing (of) the-mamluks and-we-bring-him-out with-us.
sentences.i: Bahrām said to him, “I have this Muslim here with us. We will dress him in the dress of a mamluk and bring him ashore with us.
sentences.n: anā ʿindī, 'I, with me is', the topic set first and picked up again by the suffix, a common spoken turn. albasa, Form IV, 'to clothe', takes two objects: the person (-hu) and the garment (libsa). mamālīk, 'slaves owned', the white slave-boys of the trade. nukhrijuhu, 'we bring him out', off the ship and on land.

sentences.t: وَإِذَا رَأَتْهُ الْمَلِكَةُ تَظُنُّ وَتَقُولُ هٰذَا مَمْلُوكٌ فَأَقُولُ لَهَا إِنِّي جَلَّابُ مَمَالِيكَ أَبِيعُ وَأَشْتَرِي فِيهِمْ وَقَدْ كَانَ عِنْدِي مَمَالِيكُ كَثِيرَةٌ فَبِعْتُهُمْ وَلَمْ يَبْقَ غَيْرُ هٰذَا الْمَمْلُوكِ
sentences.tr: wa-idhā raʾathu al-malikatu taẓunnu wa-taqūlu hādhā mamlūkun fa-aqūlu lahā innī jallābu mamālīka abīʿu wa-ashtarī fīhim wa-qad kāna ʿindī mamālīku kathīratun fa-biʿtuhum wa-lam yabqa ghayru hādhā al-mamlūki
sentences.l: And-when sees-him the-queen, she-will-think and-say: This (is) a-mamluk. And-I-will-say to-her: Indeed-I (am) an-importer (of) mamluks, I-sell and-I-buy in-them; and-there-had-been with-me mamluks many, and-I-sold-them, and-not remained other-than this the-mamluk.
sentences.i: When the queen sees him she will take him for a mamluk and say so, and I shall tell her that I am a dealer who brings in mamluks, buying and selling in them, that I had many of them and sold them all, and that none is left but this one.”
sentences.n: After idhā the answer comes in the plain imperfect, taẓunnu, with no fa-, a looser pattern than the Classical. jallāb, 'one who fetches (goods) from abroad', a dealer, here in slaves; mamālīka is a diptote, so genitive in -a. ishtarā fī, 'to buy and sell in, deal in': fī marks the goods traded. mamālīku kathīratun, feminine singular agreement with a broken plural, which the grammar allows even of persons, as often. The hamza of رأته and the shaddas of تظنّ and جلّاب are printed.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ لَهُ الرَّئِيسُ هٰذَا كَلَامٌ مَلِيحٌ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla lahu al-raʾīsu hādhā kalāmun malīḥun
sentences.l: And-said to-him the-captain: This (is) speech good.
sentences.i: “That is well said,” said the captain.
sentences.n: malīḥ, properly 'salty, pleasing', is the later Arabic word for 'good, fine'.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ إِنَّهُمْ وَصَلُوا إِلَى الْمَدِينَةِ وَأَرْخَوُا الْقُلُوعَ وَدَقُّوا الْمَرَاسِيَ وَوَقَفَتِ الْمَرْكَبُ
sentences.tr: thumma innahum waṣalū ilā al-madīnati wa-arkhawu al-qulūʿa wa-daqqū al-marāsiya wa-waqafati al-markabu
sentences.l: Then indeed-they arrived at the-city, and-they-let-down the-sails and-they-drove-in the-anchors, and-stood the-ship.
sentences.i: Then they reached the city, lowered the sails and dropped anchor, and the ship lay still.
sentences.n: thumma innahum, 'then they', the storyteller's thumma inna that opens a new step. arkhā, Form IV, 'to slacken, let down'; qulūʿ, 'sails', plural of qilʿ. daqqa al-marāsī, 'to drive in the anchors', marāsī being plural of mirsāh. al-markab, 'the ship', is masculine in Classical, but this text treats it as feminine, waqafat, as in fa-tāhat al-markabu earlier in the night. The shadda of دقّوا is printed.

sentences.t: وَإِذَا بِالْمَلِكَةِ مَرْجَانَةَ نَزَلَتْ عِنْدَهُمْ وَمَعَهَا عَسْكَرُهَا وَوَقَفَتْ عَلَى الْمَرْكَبِ وَنَادَتْ عَلَى الرَّئِيسِ
sentences.tr: wa-idhā bi-al-malikati Marjānata nazalat ʿindahum wa-maʿahā ʿaskaruhā wa-waqafat ʿalā al-markabi wa-nādat ʿalā al-raʾīsi
sentences.l: And-behold the-queen Marjāna came-down to-them, and-with-her her-troops; and-she-stood at the-ship and-called upon the-captain.
sentences.i: And behold, Queen Marjāna came down to them with her soldiers, stood by the ship and called for the captain.
sentences.n: wa-idhā bi-, 'and behold': the bi- after idhā of surprise only marks who appears, the queen. Marjāna, 'Coral', a woman's name and a diptote, so genitive Marjānata. nazala ʿinda, 'to come down to': the queen comes down from her castle to the harbour. nādā ʿalā, 'to call for (someone)', the later usage, where Classical has nādā with a direct object: ʿalā marks the one called. ʿaskar, 'army, troops'.

sentences.t: فَطَلَعَ عِنْدَهَا وَقَبَّلَ الْأَرْضَ بَيْنَ يَدَيْهَا
sentences.tr: fa-ṭalaʿa ʿindahā wa-qabbala al-arḍa bayna yadayhā
sentences.l: And-he-went-up to-her and-kissed the-ground between her-two-hands.
sentences.i: He went up to her and kissed the ground before her.
sentences.n: ṭalaʿa, 'to go up', here from the ship to the quay; it is the later word for leaving a ship, as nazala is for boarding one. bayna yadayhā, 'between her two hands', before her. The shadda of قبّل is printed.

sentences.t: فَقَالَتْ لَهُ أَيُّ شَيْءٌ فِي مَرْكَبِكَ هٰذِهِ وَمَنْ مَعَكَ
sentences.tr: fa-qālat lahu ayyu shayʾun fī markabika hādhihi wa-man maʿaka
sentences.l: And-she-said to-him: What thing (is) in this your-ship, and-who (is) with-you?
sentences.i: She said to him, “What is on this ship of yours, and who is with you?”
sentences.n: The print points شيءٌ in the nominative with tanwīn; after ayyu, 'which, what', Classical wants the genitive, ayyu shayʾin. Kept as printed: it perhaps reflects the spoken ayy shī, 'what?', taken as one phrase. markabika hādhihi, 'this ship of yours', with the feminine demonstrative, as the text treats markab. The shadda of ايّ is printed.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ لَهَا يَا مَلِكَةِ الزَّمَانِ مَعِي رَجُلٌ تَاجِرٌ يَبِيعُ الْمَمَالِيكَ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla lahā yā malikati al-zamāni maʿī rajulun tājirun yabīʿu al-mamālīka
sentences.l: And-he-said to-her: O queen (of) the-age, with-me (is) a-man, a-merchant, (who) sells the-mamluks.
sentences.i: “O queen of the age,” he said to her, “I have with me a merchant who sells mamluks.”
sentences.n: The print points the kasra on ملكةِ. A vocative in construct is accusative in Classical, yā malikata al-zamāni; the printed kasra is kept, and may reflect the reading aloud of the construct with a linking vowel. malikat al-zamān, 'queen of the age, of the time', the courtly address.

sentences.t: فَقَالَتْ عَلَيَّ بِهِ
sentences.tr: fa-qālat ʿalayya bihi
sentences.l: And-she-said: Upon-me with-him!
sentences.i: “Bring him to me,” she said.
sentences.n: ʿalayya bihi, 'on me with him', the set command 'bring him to me': ʿalayya, 'it is upon you to bring to me', and bi- marks the one to be brought. The shadda of عليّ is printed.

sentences.t: وَإِذَا بِبَهْرَامَ طَلَعَ وَمَعَهُ الْأَسْعَدُ مَاشٍ وَرَاءَهُ فِي صِفَةِ مَمْلُوكٍ
sentences.tr: wa-idhā bi-Bahrāma ṭalaʿa wa-maʿahu al-Asʿadu māshin warāʾahu fī ṣifati mamlūkin
sentences.l: And-behold Bahrām came-up, and-with-him al-Asʿad walking behind-him in (the) guise (of) a-mamluk.
sentences.i: And there was Bahrām, coming ashore, with al-Asʿad walking behind him in the guise of a mamluk.
sentences.n: wa-idhā bi-: the bi- after idhā of surprise only marks who appears, Bahrām; genitive in -a, as a diptote. māshin, 'walking', active participle of mashā, with the final yā dropped under tanwīn; it describes al-Asʿad's state. fī ṣifati, 'in the description of', so 'in the guise of'. The hamza of الأسعد and the ء of وراءه are printed.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا وَصَلَ إِلَيْهَا بَهْرَامُ قَبَّلَ الْأَرْضَ وَوَقَفَ بَيْنَ يَدَيْهَا
sentences.tr: fa-lammā waṣala ilayhā Bahrāmu qabbala al-arḍa wa-waqafa bayna yadayhā
sentences.l: And-when reached to-her Bahrām, he-kissed the-ground and-stood between her-two-hands.
sentences.i: When Bahrām reached her, he kissed the ground and stood before her.
sentences.n: The shadda of قبّل is printed.

sentences.t: فَقَالَتْ لَهُ مَا شَأْنُكَ
sentences.tr: fa-qālat lahu mā shaʾnuka
sentences.l: And-she-said to-him: What (is) your-affair?
sentences.i: “What is your business?” she asked him.
sentences.n: shaʾn, 'affair, business'; the print has شان with its hamza unwritten, as usual in this edition.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ لَهَا أَنَا تَاجِرُ رَقِيقِ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla lahā anā tājiru raqīqi
sentences.l: And-he-said to-her: I (am a) merchant (of) slaves.
sentences.i: “I am a slave merchant,” he said to her.
sentences.n: raqīq, 'slaves', a collective. The print points both words, تاجرُ رقيقِ: tājiru in the nominative as predicate, raqīqi genitive as the second term, with a plain kasra where Classical would put the tanwīn, raqīqin; kept as printed.

sentences.t: فَنَظَرَتْ إِلَى الْأَسْعَدِ وَقَدْ ظَنَّتْ أَنَّهُ مَمْلُوكٌ فَقَالَتْ لَهُ مَا اسْمُكَ
sentences.tr: fa-naẓarat ilā al-Asʿadi wa-qad ẓannat annahu mamlūkun fa-qālat lahu mā ismuka
sentences.l: And-she-looked at al-Asʿad, and-she-had-thought that-he (was) a-mamluk, and-she-said to-him: What (is) your-name?
sentences.i: She looked at al-Asʿad, whom she had taken for a mamluk, and said to him, “What is your name?”
sentences.n: wa-qad ẓannat, 'having thought': wa- with qad and the perfect is a circumstantial clause, 'she having taken him for'. The shadda of ظنّت is printed.

sentences.t: فَخَنَقَهُ الْبُكَاءُ وَقَالَ لَهَا اسْمِي الْأَسْعَدُ فَحَنَّ قَلْبُهَا عَلَيْهِ
sentences.tr: fa-khanaqahu al-bukāʾu wa-qāla lahā ismī al-Asʿadu fa-ḥanna qalbuhā ʿalayhi
sentences.l: And-choked-him the-weeping, and-he-said to-her: My-name (is) al-Asʿad. And-yearned her-heart towards-him.
sentences.i: Weeping choked him, and he said to her, “My name is al-Asʿad”; and her heart went out to him.
sentences.n: al-Asʿad means 'the most fortunate', which his plight belies. ḥanna ʿalā, 'to feel tenderness for': ʿalā marks the one the heart goes out to. The shadda of حنّ is printed.

sentences.t: وَقَالَتْ لَهُ أَتَعْرِفُ الْكِتَابَةَ قَالَ نَعَمْ
sentences.tr: wa-qālat lahu a-taʿrifu al-kitābata qāla naʿam
sentences.l: And-she-said to-him: Do-you-know the-writing? He-said: Yes.
sentences.i: “Do you know how to write?” she asked him. “Yes,” he said.
sentences.n: a-, the question particle, on taʿrifu. al-kitāba, 'writing', the art of the scribe and the mark of an educated man, not of a slave.

sentences.t: فَنَاوَلَتْهُ دَوَاةً وَقَلَمًا وَقِرْطَاسًا وَقَالَتْ لَهُ اكْتُبْ شَيْأً حَتَّى أَرَاهُ فَكَتَبَ هٰذَيْنِ الْبَيْتَيْنِ
sentences.tr: fa-nāwalathu dawātan wa-qalaman wa-qirṭāsan wa-qālat lahu uktub shayʾan ḥattā arāhu fa-kataba hādhayni al-baytayni
sentences.l: And-she-handed-him an-inkwell and-a-pen and-a-paper, and-she-said to-him: Write something so-that I-may-see-it. And-he-wrote these the-two-lines:
sentences.i: She handed him an inkwell, a pen and a sheet of paper and said to him, “Write something, so that I may see it”; and he wrote these two lines:
sentences.n: nāwala, Form III, 'to hand over', with two objects. qirṭās, 'paper, a sheet'. ḥattā with the subjunctive, arāhu, 'so that I may see it'. The print spells shayʾan as شيأ, its usual spelling; kept as set.

sentences.t:
مَا حَيْلَةُ الْمَرْأُ وَالْاَقْدَارُ جَارِيَةٌ * عَلَيْهِ فِي كُلِّ حَالِ اَيُّهَا الرَّائِي
اَلْقَاهُ فِي الْيَمِّ مَكْتُوفًا وَقَالَ لَهُ * اِيَّاكَ اِيَّاكَ اَنْ تَبْتَلَّ بِالْمَاءِ
sentences.tr:
mā ḥaylatu al-marʾu wa-al-aqdāru jāriyatun * ʿalayhi fī kulli ḥāli ayyuhā al-rāʾī
alqāhu fī al-yammi maktūfan wa-qāla lahu * iyyāka iyyāka an tabtalla bi-al-māʾi
sentences.l:
What (is the) device (of) the-man, while-the-decrees (are) running against-him in every state, O you-the-onlooker?
He-threw-him into the-sea bound, and-said to-him: Beware, beware that you-get-wet with-the-water!
sentences.i:
What can a man contrive, O you who look on, when the decrees run against him in every state?
He flung him bound into the sea, and said to him: “Take care, take care you do not get wet!”
sentences.n: Metre basīṭ, both lines. The print points both lines; the pointing is kept as set, though two vowels are not the Classical ones: حَيْلَةُ, with a fatḥa, for ḥīlatu, 'device, stratagem', and الْمَرْأُ, nominative, where the construct after ḥīlatu wants the genitive, al-marʾi. The metre allows either. wa-al-aqdāru jāriyatun, 'the decrees running', a circumstantial clause: fate's decrees run against him whatever his state. The second line is a widely quoted image of fate, often credited to the mystic al-Ḥallāj: the one who casts a man bound into the sea and forbids him to get wet. al-yamm, 'the sea', a Qurʾānic word. iyyāka … an, 'beware of …': the warning iyyāka governs the an-clause. al-Asʿad writes his own case: thrown into captivity, then told to play the slave.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا رَأَتِ الْوَرَقَةَ رَحِمَتْهُ ثُمَّ قَالَتْ لِبَهْرَامَ بِعْنِي هٰذَا الْمَمْلُوكَ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā raʾati al-waraqata raḥimathu thumma qālat li-Bahrāma biʿnī hādhā al-mamlūka
sentences.l: And-when she-saw the-paper, she-pitied-him; then she-said to-Bahrām: Sell-me this the-mamluk.
sentences.i: When she saw the paper she took pity on him, and she said to Bahrām, “Sell me this mamluk.”
sentences.n: biʿnī, 'sell (to) me', imperative of bāʿa with the buyer as direct object. li-Bahrāma: li- marks the one spoken to. The hamza of رأت is printed.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ لَهَا يَا سِتِّي لَا يُمْكِنُنِي بَيْعُهُ لِأَنِّي بِعْتُ جَمِيعَ مَمَالِيكِي وَلَمْ يَبْقَ عِنْدِي غَيْرُ هٰذَا
sentences.tr: fa-qāla lahā yā sittī lā yumkinunī bayʿuhu li-annī biʿtu jamīʿa mamālīkī wa-lam yabqa ʿindī ghayru hādhā
sentences.l: And-he-said to-her: O my-lady, not is-possible-for-me (the) selling-(of)-him, because-I sold all (of) my-mamluks, and-not remained with-me other-than this.
sentences.i: “My lady,” he said to her, “I cannot sell him, for I have sold all my mamluks, and this one is all I have left.”
sentences.n: sittī, 'my lady', the later Arabic form of sayyidatī. lā yumkinunī bayʿuhu, 'his sale is not possible for me': bayʿuhu, the verbal noun, is the subject. li-anna, 'because': li- gives the reason. The shadda of لانّي is printed.

sentences.t: فَقَالَتِ الْمَلِكَةُ مَرْجَانَةُ لَابُدَّ مِنْ أَخْذِهِ مِنْكَ إِمَّا بِبَيْعٍ وَإِمَّا بِهِبَةٍ
sentences.tr: fa-qālati al-malikatu Marjānatu lā budda min akhdhihi minka immā bi-bayʿin wa-immā bi-hibatin
sentences.l: And-said the-queen Marjāna: No escape from (the) taking-(of)-him from-you, either by-sale or by-gift.
sentences.i: Queen Marjāna said, “I must have him from you, either by sale or as a gift.”
sentences.n: lā budda min, 'there is no escape from', so 'it must be'; printed as one word, لابد, kept as set. immā … wa-immā, 'either … or'; bi- is 'by (way of)'. bayʿ / hiba, sale and gift, the two ways property passes. The shadda of امّا is printed, both times.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ لَهَا لَا أَبِيعُهُ وَلَا أَهَبُهُ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla lahā lā abīʿuhu wa-lā ahabuhu
sentences.l: And-he-said to-her: Not I-sell-him and-not I-give-him.
sentences.i: “I will neither sell him nor give him away,” he said to her.
sentences.n: ahabu, from wahaba, 'to give', whose wāw drops in the imperfect.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ مَسَكَتْ بِيَدِ الْأَسْعَدِ وَأَخَذَتْهُ وَطَلَعَتْ بِهِ الْقَلْعَةَ
sentences.tr: thumma masakat bi-yadi al-Asʿadi wa-akhadhathu wa-ṭalaʿat bihi al-qalʿata
sentences.l: Then she-held by-(the)-hand (of) al-Asʿad, and-took-him, and-went-up with-him (to) the-castle.
sentences.i: Then she took al-Asʿad by the hand, led him away and went up with him to the castle.
sentences.n: masaka bi-, 'to take hold of', the later Arabic for Classical amsaka bi-: bi- marks what is grasped. ṭalaʿa bihi al-qalʿata, 'she went up with him to the castle': bi- marks the one taken along, and the place is a direct object without a preposition, a spoken usage.

sentences.t: وَأَرْسَلَتْ تَقُولُ لَهُ إِنْ لَمْ تُقْلِعْ فِي هٰذِهِ اللَّيْلَةِ عَنْ بَلَدِنَا أَخَذْتُ جَمِيعَ مَالِكَ وَكَسَرْتُ مَرْكَبَكَ
sentences.tr: wa-arsalat taqūlu lahu in lam tuqliʿ fī hādhihi al-laylati ʿan baladinā akhadhtu jamīʿa mālika wa-kasartu markabaka
sentences.l: And-she-sent saying to-him: If not you-set-sail in this the-night from our-land, I-take all (of) your-wealth and-I-break your-ship.
sentences.i: And she sent to tell him, “If you do not sail from our land this very night, I shall seize all your goods and wreck your ship.”
sentences.n: arsalat taqūlu, 'she sent, saying', the imperfect giving the message the sender bears. aqlaʿa ʿan, Form IV, 'to set sail from': ʿan marks the place left. After in the perfects akhadhtu and kasartu have future sense, 'I shall take, I shall break'. The ḍamma of اخذتُ is printed, marking the first person.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا وَصَلَتْ إِلَيْهِ الرِّسَالَةِ اهْتَمَّ هَمًّا شَدِيدًا وَقَالَ إِنَّ هٰذِهِ سَفْرَةٌ غَيْرُ مَحْمُودَةٍ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā waṣalat ilayhi al-risālati ihtamma hamman shadīdan wa-qāla inna hādhihi safratun ghayru maḥmūdatin
sentences.l: And-when reached to-him the-message, he-was-troubled (with) a-trouble severe, and-he-said: Indeed this (is) a-voyage not praised.
sentences.i: When the message reached him he was sorely troubled, and said, “This is an ill-starred voyage.”
sentences.n: The print points الرسالةِ with a kasra; as the subject of waṣalat it should be nominative, al-risālatu. Kept as printed, perhaps a slip of the pointing. ihtamma hamman shadīdan, 'he grieved a severe grief', the verb strengthened by its own verbal noun (mafʿūl muṭlaq). ghayr maḥmūda, 'not praiseworthy', ill-omened. The shaddas of اهتمّ and همّا are printed.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ قَامَ وَتَجَهَّزَ وَأَخَذَ جَمِيعَ مَا يُرِيدُهُ وَانْتَظَرَ اللَّيْلَ يُقْبِلُ عَلَيْهِ لِيُسَافِرَ فِيهِ
sentences.tr: thumma qāma wa-tajahhaza wa-akhadha jamīʿa mā yurīduhu wa-intaẓara al-layla yuqbilu ʿalayhi li-yusāfira fīhi
sentences.l: Then he-rose and-made-ready and-took all (of) what he-wants-it, and-he-awaited the-night coming upon-him, so-that-he-might-travel in-it.
sentences.i: Then he rose and made ready, took everything he needed, and waited for night to come on, so that he might sail under cover of it.
sentences.n: intaẓara al-layla yuqbilu, 'he awaited the night coming on': the imperfect describes the night as awaited. li- with the subjunctive, li-yusāfira, 'so that he might travel'. The shadda of تجهّز is printed.

sentences.t: وَقَالَ لِلْبَحْرِيَّةِ خُذُوا أُهْبَتَكُمْ وَامْلَؤُا قِرَبَكُمْ مِنَ الْمَاءِ وَأَقْلِعُوا بِنَا فِي آخِرِ اللَّيْلِ
sentences.tr: wa-qāla li-al-baḥriyyati khudhū uhbatakum wa-imlaʾū qirabakum mina al-māʾi wa-aqliʿū binā fī ākhiri al-layli
sentences.l: And-he-said to-the-sailors: Take your-gear and-fill your-waterskins from the-water, and-set-sail with-us in (the) end (of) the-night.
sentences.i: And he said to the sailors, “Get your gear together, fill your waterskins, and set sail with us at the end of the night.”
sentences.n: al-baḥriyya, 'the sea-folk', the crew, a collective; li- marks the ones spoken to. uhba, 'readiness, equipment'. qirab, plural of qirba, 'waterskin'; min marks what they are filled with. aqliʿū binā, 'sail with us': bi- marks those carried along. The print spells the imperative واملؤا with a final alif after the wāw of the plural, the usual spelling; the ؤ and the madda of آخر are printed.

sentences.t: فَصَارَ الْبَحْرِيَّةُ يَقْضُونَ أَشْغَالَهُمْ وَيَنْتَظِرُونَ اللَّيْلَ فَأَقْبَلَ اللَّيْلُ عَلَيْهِمْ
sentences.tr: fa-ṣāra al-baḥriyyatu yaqḍūna ashghālahum wa-yantaẓirūna al-layla fa-aqbala al-laylu ʿalayhim
sentences.l: And-began the-sailors finishing their-tasks and-awaiting the-night; and-came-on the-night upon-them.
sentences.i: So the sailors set about their tasks and waited for night, and night came on.
sentences.n: ṣāra with an imperfect, 'they set about, began to', the later Arabic sense. The verb is singular before its subject and the plural yaqḍūna follows it, al-baḥriyya being a collective taken as plural. qaḍā ashghālahu, 'to get one's jobs done'.

sentences.t: هٰذَا مَا كَانَ مِنْ أَمْرِهِمْ
sentences.tr: hādhā mā kāna min amrihim
sentences.l: This (is) what was of their-affair.
sentences.i: So much for them.
sentences.n: The storyteller's formula of transition, as in the last night.

sentences.t: وَأَمَّا مَا كَانَ مِنْ أَمْرِ الْمَلِكَةِ مَرْجَانَةَ فَإِنَّهَا أَخَذَتِ الْأَسْعَدَ وَدَخَلَتْ بِهِ إِلَى الْقَلْعَةِ وَفَتَحَتِ الشَّبَابِيكَ الْمُطِلَّةَ عَلَى الْبَحْرِ
sentences.tr: wa-ammā mā kāna min amri al-malikati Marjānata fa-innahā akhadhati al-Asʿada wa-dakhalat bihi ilā al-qalʿati wa-fataḥati al-shabābīka al-muṭillata ʿalā al-baḥri
sentences.l: And-as-for what was of (the) affair (of) the-queen Marjāna, then-indeed-she took al-Asʿad and-entered with-him into the-castle, and-opened the-windows overlooking upon the-sea.
sentences.i: As for Queen Marjāna, she took al-Asʿad and went with him into the castle, and opened the windows that looked out over the sea.
sentences.n: dakhala bihi, 'she went in with him': bi- marks the one taken along. shabābīk, plural of shubbāk, 'window'. aṭalla ʿalā, Form IV, 'to look down over': the participle muṭilla, 'overlooking', agrees with the plural of things as a feminine singular; its shadda is printed.

sentences.t: وَأَمَرَتِ الْجَوَارِيَ أَنْ يُقَدِّمْنَ الطَّعَامَ فَقَدَّمْنَ لَهُمَا الطَّعَامَ فَأَكَلَا
sentences.tr: wa-amarati al-jawāriya an yuqaddimna al-ṭaʿāma fa-qaddamna lahumā al-ṭaʿāma fa-akalā
sentences.l: And-she-ordered the-slave-girls that they-bring-forward the-food; and-they-brought-forward for-the-two-of-them the-food, and-the-two-ate.
sentences.i: She ordered the slave-girls to serve the food, and they served it to the two of them, and the two of them ate.
sentences.n: jawārī, plural of jāriya, 'slave-girl'. an with the subjunctive, here the feminine plural yuqaddimna, which shows no ending. lahumā, 'for the two of them': li- marks those served; the dual runs on in akalā, 'the two ate'.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ أَمَرَتْهُنَّ أَنْ يُقَدِّمْنَ الْمُدَامَ
sentences.tr: thumma amarathunna an yuqaddimna al-mudāma
sentences.l: Then she-ordered-them that they-bring-forward the-wine.
sentences.i: Then she ordered them to bring the wine.
sentences.n: mudām, 'wine', properly 'what is kept long (in the jar)', a poetic word for wine.

sentences.t: وَأَدْرَكَ شَهْرَزَادَ الصَّبَاحُ فَسَكَتَتْ عَنِ الْكَلَامِ الْمُبَاحِ
sentences.tr: wa-adraka Shahrazāda al-ṣabāḥu fa-sakatat ʿani al-kalāmi al-mubāḥi
sentences.l: And the-morning overtook Shahrazād, and-she-fell-silent from the-permitted speech.
sentences.i: And morning overtook Shahrazād, and she fell silent from the speech allowed her.
sentences.n: The closing formula, as at the end of every night. The rhyme falls on al-ṣabāḥ / al-mubāḥ.
